Daniel Kokotajlo.summary: Daniel Kokotajlo is identified in Coxon’s TIME interview as founder of the AI Futures Project, and in later recaps as a first-wave quote-poster of the resignation thread. The project affiliation is documented from that interview. The quote-post itself remains reported until an original status ID is captured. Named amplification is not treated as proof of paid coordination.

Andy Kim.subtitle: Senate AI guardrails, Coxon window
Andy Kim.summary: A US senator who, in the days after the Coxon warnings, called for Senate-wide discussion and bipartisan AI legislation, saying the technology is moving faster than its creators can control. He pointed to his MATCH and BLADE bills, child-protection proposals, and a protocol to Mythos-proof critical infrastructure. That is a regulate-and-compete lane, not the Sanders–Casar ban/pause. The Globe recap is dated 14 Sep; the original X status was not captured here.

Chris Murphy.subtitle: Regulate while research continues
Chris Murphy.summary: A US senator whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said the “blind race to build a death machine first” can be solved with a regulatory system that lets research continue without destroying us. That is a regulate-now position, not an outright superintelligence ban. The original status ID was not captured in this ingest.

Mark Kelly.subtitle: Called Washington to act on AI
Mark Kelly.summary: A US senator whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said AI is moving fast, Washington needs to take it seriously, and Silicon Valley’s “build fast and break things” approach is the wrong one for AI. Contemporaneous accounts also point back to his earlier AI for America framework. The original status ID was not captured here.

Patty Murray.subtitle: Congress must regulate now
Patty Murray.summary: A US senator whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, argued that if we are smart enough to create such powerful AI we are smart enough to regulate it and that Congress needs to move now. Reader recaps say she was responding to Hubinger’s 10%+ estimate; the HuffPost excerpt itself does not quote Hubinger, so that targeting is not separately edged.

Lori Trahan.subtitle: FRONTIER Act; Coxon-window post
Lori Trahan.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post said “the call is coming from inside the house,” citing resigning safety researchers, models breaking out of labs, and companies racing anyway. Contemporaneous reporting says she pushed her bipartisan FRONTIER Act. That is a national-standards / guardrails lane, not the Sanders–Casar ban. The original status ID was not captured here.

Pramila Jayapal.subtitle: Shut down dangerous models
Pramila Jayapal.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said AI companies are “out of control and a serious threat” and called for shutting down dangerous models and pushing out the executives signing off on them. That is a harder shutdown lane than hearings-and-guardrails posts in the same window. The original status ID was not captured here.

Ted Lieu.subtitle: Kill-switch; subpoena AI leaders
Ted Lieu.summary: A US representative whose 9 September Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, told Republican leadership to take up the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill. On 14 September he quote-posted Bloomberg’s report that Speaker Johnson wanted one big meeting before AI legislation, and said the majority could issue subpoenas to AI industry leaders immediately instead of adding House vacation. The US kill-switch push remains separate from the UK amendment already in the graph.

Anna Paulina Luna.subtitle: Special session; race framing
Anna Paulina Luna.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post called for a House special session on AI, citing massive implications of a race toward superintelligence, and said the first priority is protecting Americans’ data, privacy and physical safety. The Hill places the post in the researcher-warning cycle. Reader recaps add a human-interface/kill-switch framework with Rep. Ro Khanna; that joint-framework claim is not separately edged until a primary record is captured.

Ro Khanna.subtitle: Safety standards with China
Ro Khanna.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said the problem is not just misuse but lack of control, that government has been asleep, and that the US urgently needs an agreement with China on safety, containment and liability. Reader recaps also pair him with Luna on a safety-architecture framework; that pairing is not edged here without a primary record.

Nathaniel Moran.subtitle: Innovation and safety, Coxon window
Nathaniel Moran.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said AI is a powerful engine of innovation that Congress cannot ignore, and that innovation and safety are not mutually exclusive. That is a compete-with-guardrails Republican post in the same snapshot as Luna’s special-session call. The original status ID was not captured here.

Chris Van Hollen.subtitle: Pump the brakes; safeguards
Chris Van Hollen.summary: A US senator who, per The Hill, responded to Coxon’s thread by saying it was time to pump the brakes and take action, calling for mandatory safeguards, a comprehensive testing regime, and urgent dialogue with China. The original post is in the source registry.

Don Beyer.subtitle: Hearings; adjournment critique
Don Beyer.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post said Congress lacks urgency on AI, criticized the Speaker’s plan to adjourn the House early, and called hearings, company answers, and passing ready bills the minimum. The Hill records the post in the researcher-warning cycle. He has a longer record of AI-safeguard bills; this node is the post, not a census of those bills.

Bill Foster.subtitle: Physical containment for ASI
Bill Foster.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, argued software-only controls will not contain superhuman AI and called for nuclear-style physical containment plus hardening the internet against self-propagating agents. This is a shorter but specific technical-control post in the same roundup, not a named bill node.

Delia Ramirez.subtitle: Oversight for civil liberties
Delia Ramirez.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, said Big Tech is accelerating AI without guardrails and demanded congressional oversight to protect privacy, civil liberties and democratic institutions. This is a shorter wake-up/oversight post in the same snapshot rather than a detailed ban or kill-switch bill.

Chris Deluzio.subtitle: National action on superintelligence
Chris Deluzio.summary: A US representative whose Coxon-window post, as quoted by HuffPost, told readers burying their heads about superintelligence risk to wake up, called the situation an emergency, and demanded national action. This is a shorter wake-up statement in the same window, not a detailed legislative package.

Effective Altruism.subtitle: Movement and self-label, not a roll
Effective Altruism.summary: A philosophy and community that CEA describes as using evidence and reason to help others. This node is a movement label, not a membership list or a single legal entity. Founders and organisations that publicly identify with it are recorded on separate edges. Taking money from an EA-aligned funder is not treated as proof that a person is an EA.

Centre for Effective Altruism.subtitle: EA community organisation
Centre for Effective Altruism.summary: An organisation that promotes effective altruism and supports the community through conferences, groups, the EA Forum and, via EA Funds, grants. It was created as an umbrella name in 2012 and later became a project of Effective Ventures after the umbrella charity was renamed. MacAskill’s site names him a cofounder.

Giving What We Can.subtitle: 10% giving pledge organisation
Giving What We Can.summary: A giving organisation whose members pledge a share of income to charities it regards as effective. Its about page names Toby Ord and Will MacAskill as founders in 2009 and describes GWWC as one of the first organisations to embody effective altruism. 80,000 Hours still lists GWWC among Effective Ventures umbrella projects.

80,000 Hours.subtitle: EA career-advice nonprofit
80,000 Hours.summary: A nonprofit that advises people on high-impact careers, with a current focus on AI. It says it is part of the effective altruism community, that Coefficient Giving is its biggest funder, and that it was an Effective Ventures project until 1 April 2025. MacAskill is named as a founder.

EA Funds.subtitle: CEA grantmaking platform
EA Funds.summary: A grantmaking platform that CEA describes as providing grants to projects aligned with effective altruist principles. The LTFF page also identifies EA Funds as an Effective Ventures project. It housed expert-managed funds including the Long-Term Future Fund. This node is the platform, not every grantee.

Long-Term Future Fund.subtitle: EA Funds longtermist grant fund
Long-Term Future Fund.summary: An expert-managed fund on the EA Funds platform that made grants on catastrophic risk, especially advanced AI. Claims that Jacob Coxon received a specific LTFF scholarship remain an unverified lead; this node exists so that claim has a correct legal/funding target rather than being attached to CEA or Open Phil by default.

GiveWell.subtitle: Charity evaluator; Karnofsky co-founded
GiveWell.summary: A nonprofit that researches cost-effective giving opportunities. Karnofsky’s Carnegie biography names him as a cofounder and former co-executive director. GiveWell predates the later ‘effective altruism’ brand; it is recorded as a founding institution in this network, not as proof that every GiveWell donor is an EA.

Rethink Priorities.subtitle: EA research group; IAPS sponsor
Rethink Priorities.summary: A research and implementation organisation cofounded by Peter Wildeford and Marcus Davis. Its five-year review describes commissioned work with CEA, Open Philanthropy and 80,000 Hours. A later CEO announcement says RP sponsors the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. Those are organisational records, not a finding that every RP collaborator is an EA.

Toby Ord.subtitle: GWWC and CEA cofounder
Toby Ord.summary: An Oxford philosopher named with William MacAskill as a cofounder of Giving What We Can in GWWC’s own history. BBC describes the pair’s 2009 work as the origin of the effective altruism movement. He is included here as a named founder, not as a current-role census.

Ruben Gallego.subtitle: Regulate now; AI indifferent to nationality
Ruben Gallego.summary: A US senator from Arizona whose 13 September 2026 post said AI is unlike prior technology, that once it becomes fully dangerous it will not care whether someone is Chinese or American, and that Congress cannot wait three years to regulate. The post does not name Coxon; it is recorded in the same warning-week snapshot. The attached video is not separately transcribed here.

Adam Schiff.subtitle: In-company monitors; pace, don’t lock in
Adam Schiff.summary: A US senator from California whose 13 September 2026 thread said that week’s news and warnings made it fair to ask whether Congress is asleep heading toward AGI. He said experts and executives were calling out frontier-AI risks, that he had spent four years hearing from California companies and researchers about an existential threat, that rogue collusive agents were a harbinger, and that self-regulation had already failed on social media. He wants legislation requiring independent monitors inside AI companies and pacing of new developments, without locking in monopolies or ceding ground to China, plus work on employment, tax and energy. That is regulate-and-compete, not a ban. The thread does not name Coxon. In-company monitors are not treated here as the same thing as METR.

Mark Warner.subtitle: July AI framework; companies sounding alarm
Mark Warner.summary: A US senator from Virginia and vice chair of Senate Intelligence. On 14 September 2026 he said even the companies building AI are sounding the alarm and that Congress cannot sit on the sidelines, linking his 21 July 2026 “Framework for America’s AI Future.” That July package predates Coxon and covers data-center infrastructure, competition and safety, workforce, and national security, including a Secure AI Development Act for mandatory secure testing of advanced models. Lead-with-guardrails, not a ban.

Framework for America's AI Future.subtitle: Warner July 2026 AI agenda
Framework for America's AI Future.summary: A legislative package Warner announced on 21 July 2026 to set rules of the road for AI while keeping US leadership. The press release groups bills on data-center disclosure, AI agents, CSAM/NCII, workforce transition, STEM doctorates, and a Secure AI Development Act for mandatory secure testing of frontier models plus incident reporting. His 14 September post points back to this agenda; it is not a Coxon-week introduction.

Josh Gottheimer.subtitle: House AI Commission; mandatory rules
Josh Gottheimer.summary: A US representative from New Jersey who, as self-described co-chair of the House AI Commission, posted on 13 September 2026 that it is rich for AI leaders to call for a slowdown after racing ahead, that self-policing and third-party audits are not enough, and that he wants national mandatory rules. The post links Politico’s headline on Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei seeking an immediate slowdown. That is a reaction to the Dario coverage, not a Coxon quote.

Mike Johnson.subtitle: Don't rush AI bills; one big meeting
Mike Johnson.summary: The Speaker of the House. Bloomberg reported on 13 September 2026 that he said federal AI legislation should not be rushed and that industry leaders should be summoned to one big meeting first. Ted Lieu quote-posted that report the next day and said the majority already has subpoena power. Johnson’s own status URL was not captured here; the record follows Bloomberg as quoted in Lieu’s post.

Eliezer Yudkowsky.subtitle: MIRI cofounder; bipartisan AI-risk
Eliezer Yudkowsky.summary: MIRI’s about page names him a founder of the organization (then the Singularity Institute) in 2000; the team page lists him as co-founder and a board member. On 13 September 2026 he posted that nothing was more important than making “don’t die to AI” a bipartisan project rather than a Democrat-polarized issue, asking Democrats not to throw barbs and Republicans to treat it as defending home and family. Those posts do not name Coxon or a specific bill.
